quote: When Dade County forbade use or possession of phosphate detergents, many Dade residents drove to nearby counties and bought huge amounts of phosphate laundry detergents. Compared to Tampa residents not affected by the regulation, Dade residents rated phosphate detergents as gentler, more effective, more powerful on stains, and even believed that phosphate detergents poured more easily.
content: The Mazis studies are surveys of a few hundred housewives in Miami and Tampa, compared cross-sectionally after the ban, with no pre-ban baseline and no random assignment. The design cannot separate reactance from two obvious alternatives. First, selection: the Miami respondents who still had opinions about phosphate detergents included the ones who had driven to Broward County to buy them, and people who have made an effort to obtain something rate it highly, which is the effort-justification effect this book describes elsewhere. Second, city differences: Miami and Tampa differed in water hardness, income and demographics in ways that plausibly affect detergent preference, and “Tampa residents not affected by the regulation” is a comparison group, not a control group. Mazis reported the difference as reactance because reactance was the hypothesis; the data are equally consistent with the people who wanted phosphates most being the ones who noticed the ban most. The finding is repeated in every edition of Cialdini and has not, to my knowledge, been replicated with a design that could distinguish these explanations.

quote: If the judge afterward informed the jurors that information about insurance was inadmissible and must be ignored, jurors awarded an average of thirteen thousand dollars more than if the driver had no insurance.
content: The backfire effect of an instruction to disregard is the memorable finding of the Chicago Jury Project, and it is not the general case. The meta-analysis of forty-eight studies of inadmissible evidence (Steblay et al. (2006)) found that jurors who receive an instruction to disregard move their verdicts part of the way back toward what they would have decided without the evidence; the instruction is imperfect but it works on average, and the backfire appears only under particular conditions, chiefly when the reason given for exclusion is a legal technicality that jurors regard as unjust rather than a reason bearing on reliability. Broeder’s 1959 result was a single condition in a mock-jury paradigm with small cells, reported in a law review without inferential statistics, and it became a textbook fact by repetition through Cialdini. The essay reports it as a demonstration of scarcity making forbidden information weightier; the literature that followed found that forbidding usually makes it weigh less, and that the direction depends on why the jurors think it was forbidden.

quote: Buyers told that beef was in scarce supply, and furthermore, that the information about scarcity was itself scarce—that the shortage was not general knowledge—ordered six times as much beef. (Since the study was conducted in a real-world context, the information provided was in fact correct.)
content: Set aside that the source is an unpublished dissertation known only through Cialdini’s summary. The behaviour described is not a bias. A wholesale buyer who receives credible private information that a commodity is about to become scarce, and that competitors do not yet know it, should buy more, because the price will rise when the information becomes public; that is the definition of trading on private information, and the parenthesis concedes that the information was true. The buyers’ six-fold order is the rational response of a merchant to an informational advantage, and the fact that the “exclusive information” condition produced a larger response than the “scarcity” condition is what one would expect if the buyers were reasoning about prices rather than reacting to a threat to their freedom. Cialdini presents the study as a demonstration of the scarcity principle acting on professionals; a demonstration of a bias needs a case in which the response is wrong, and the only case in this essay in which the information was real is the one in which the response was right.

quote: The fundamental instincts involved appear to be preservation of status and preservation of options.
content: Three different theories are compressed into a single “instinct” and then given an ancestral story. Reactance theory (Brehm 1966; measurement in Dillard & Shen (2005)) is about threatened freedom and predicts effects only when an agent is seen to be restricting choice; commodity theory (Brock 1968; meta-analysis in Lynn (1991)) is about unavailability raising valuation regardless of agency, and Lynn found the effect present mainly when the scarce item was already assumed desirable; loss aversion and the endowment effect (Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler 1990) explain the toddler and the appliance customer without either. Which mechanism operates in which of Cialdini’s demonstrations is unresolved, “preservation of status” is not part of any of the three, and the hunter-gatherer sentence is a just-so story of the type Book III’s annotations found the book warning against and then telling. The behavioural regularity is real enough to sell appliances; the essay’s account of what it is and where it came from is an inference from the fact that it exists.
